The CH conversion process involves the deconstruction of triglyceride-based feedstocks (e.g., seed oils, animal oils, fats, greases) into hydrocarbons via exposure to catalysts in the presence of supercritical or near-supercritical water. The multistep CH conversion process is shown in Figure 14, involving discrete preconditioning, conversion, and refining stages. During the preconditioning steps that include conjugation, cyclization, and crosslinking chemistry, the chemical backbone of the triglyceride feedstock is catalytically altered to prepare the fatty acid chains for subsequent conversion, a crucial step that prevents the excessive formation of light gases and maximizes the yield to jet range hydrocarbons (Eswaran et al. 2021). After preconditioning, exposure to high-temperature, high-pressure water facilitates cracking, deoxygenation, and cyclization chemistries to generate a broad, more petroleum-like distribution of hydrocarbons, including a mixture of paraffins, isoparaffins, cycloalkanes, and importantly a tunable fraction—typically 5% to 25%—of aromatics. This produced aromatic fraction is a key differentiator from other SAF pathways which typically must blend with petroleum-based jet to meet specifications. The aromatic fraction is a necessary ingredient of SAF that plays a critical role to (1) swell aircraft elastomer seals, (2) improve volumetric energy content, and (3) optimize lubricity and viscosity. Overview of the CH process While on the surface CH resembles the HEFA pathway in that it is similarly based on the cracking of triglyceride feedstocks, CH is considered to be more tolerant of impurities, moisture, and composition. Specifically, whereas HEFA typically requires clean, refined oils and extensive feed purification to protect the activity and lifetime of the hydrotreating catalysts, CH’s hydrothermal environment and fundamentally different chemical process is comparatively more tolerant of impurities, allowing the use of high-free-fatty-acid ‘brown’ greases, animal fats, wet algae oils, and other lower-grade streams with minimal pretreatment. These less stringent purity requirements for CH feedstocks minimize the need for costlier pre-conversion cleanup and enhance overall feedstock flexibility to support commercialization and scale-up. 18 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. Despite the various promising aspects of the CH pathway, it has not yet been deployed at significant scale. The high temperatures and high pressures required to generate supercritical water can drive up both operating and capital costs due to lower efficiency and more demanding metallurgical and maintenance requirements. Further, the generation of water-rich waste streams require more extensive and costlier cleanup than in some other pathways. Ultimately, when viewed against similar triglyceride-based pathways (e.g., HEFA), currently HEFA benefits from a first-mover advantage and direct linkage to the established commercial renewable diesel market; additionally, HEFA is more commercially practiced because of the more mature technical pathway, compatibility with existing decades-old renewable diesel infrastructure, and clearer and established offtake pathways from multiple providers (e.g., Neste, UOP, Eni, Chevron, Marathon, Philips66, Holly Energy).
